claim: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a severe birth defect characterized by incomplete formation or muscularization of the diaphragm and herniation of abdominal organs into the pulmonary cavities, leading to pulmonary hypoplasia.
source: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a severe birth defect, characterized by incomplete formation or muscularization of the diaphragm and, as a consequence, herniation of the stomach, intestines, liver or spleen into the pulmonary cavities, leading to pulmonary hypoplasia.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about CDH that draws from established medical knowledge and is supported by citations in the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: CDH occurs approximately in 1 out of 3000 births, accounting for about 8% of all severe congenital anomalies.
source: CDH occurs approximately in 1 out of 3000 births, accounting for about 8% of all severe congenital anomalies.
evidence: This is an epidemiological statistic about CDH prevalence that represents established medical knowledge.

claim: 80–90% of all CDH cases are posterolateral hernias, also known as Bochdalek-type CDH, characterized by a defect in the posterolateral area of the diaphragm.
source: 80–90% of all the cases are posterolateral hernias, also known as Bochdalek-type CDH, characterized by a defect in the postero (dorsal in mice) lateral area of the diaphragm.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Pober et al., 2010 in the manuscript and represents established medical knowledge.

claim: In most cases (>85%), Bochdalek-type CDH is located at the left side.
source: In most cases (>85%), this defect is located at the left side (Pober et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pober et al., 2010.

claim: The classical hypothesis is that Bochdalek CDH is due to a failure of the fusion of pleuroperitoneal folds (PPFs) with the septum transversum (ST).
source: The classical hypothesis is that Bochdalek CDH is due to a failure of the fusion of pleuroperitoneal folds (PPFs) with the septum transversum (ST).
evidence: This statement describes a classical hypothesis in the field, supported by citation to Mayer et al., 2011.

claim: PPFs are lateral rims of tissue connecting caudally with the nephric ridges and anteriorly with the ST.
source: PPFs are lateral rims of tissue connecting caudally with the nephric ridges and anteriorly with the ST (Mayer et al., 2011).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by citation to Mayer et al., 2011.

claim: Some authors describe that fusion rather occurs with the posthepatic mesenchymal plate (PHMP), an accumulation of mesenchymal cells derived from the ST and located in the posterodorsal margin of the liver lobes.
source: Some authors describe that this fusion rather occurs with the posthepatic mesenchymal plate (PHMP), an accumulation of mesenchymal cells derived from the ST and located in the posterodorsal margin of the liver lobes (Iritani et al., 1984).
evidence: This alternative anatomical description is supported by citation to Iritani et al., 1984.

claim: Deletion of GATA4 in the PPFs mesenchyme using a Prrx1Cre driver leads to the development of amuscular, weak areas in the diaphragm and CDH in mice.
source: Recently, it has been described in mice that deletion of GATA4 in the PPFs mesenchyme using a Prrx1Cre driver leads to the development of amuscular, weak areas in the diaphragm and CDH (Merrell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Merrell et al., 2015.

claim: The Prrx1Cre;Gata4fl/fl phenotype does not display diaphragmatic discontinuities, neither does it show a prevalence on the left side, which are common features in human CDH.
source: However, this report does not distinguish between PPFs and PHMP and the phenotype does not display diaphragmatic discontinuities, neither does it show a prevalence on the left side, which are common features in human CDH.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited work of Merrell et al., 2015, comparing their findings to human CDH characteristics.

claim: Nitrofen treatment leads to reduced size of the PPFs/PHMP, especially in the left side, decreasing cell proliferation in this area.
source: It has been shown that nitrofen treatment leads to reduced size of the PPFs/PHMP, especially in the left side, decreasing cell proliferation in this area (Clugston and Green, 2007; Clugston et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clugston and Green, 2007 and Clugston et al., 2010.

claim: Nitrofen treatment decreases expression of WT1 and GATA4 in the nitrofen model of CDH.
source: It has been shown that nitrofen treatment leads to reduced size of the PPFs/PHMP, especially in the left side, decreasing cell proliferation in this area (Clugston and Green, 2007; Clugston et al., 2010) and also decreasing expression of WT1 and GATA4 (Dingeman et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dingeman et al., 2011, 2013.

claim: RA treatment in the nitrofen model partially rescues the pulmonary hypoplasia defect.
source: RA treatment in this model partially rescues the pulmonary hypoplasia defect (Montedonico et al., 2008; Sugimoto et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montedonico et al., 2008 and Sugimoto et al., 2008.

claim: Only a few examples of CDH in humans have been associated to mutations in WT1 locus, such as the Denys-Drash, Meacham and WAGR syndromes.
source: To date, only a few examples of CDH in human have been associated to mutations in WT1 locus, such as the Denys-Drash, Meacham and WAGR syndromes (Scott et al., 2005; Suri et al., 2007; Antonius et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scott et al., 2005; Suri et al., 2007; Antonius et al., 2008.

claim: WT1 is expressed in the coelomic epithelium of the septum transversum of mouse embryos by the stage E9.0.
source: WT1 is expressed in the coelomic epithelium of the septum transversum of mouse embryos by the stage E9.0.
evidence: This is a statement about WT1 expression pattern that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of function of the Wilms' tumor suppressor gene Wt1 in mice leads to defective diaphragms.
source: Loss of function of the Wilms' tumor suppressor gene Wt1 in mice leads to defective diaphragms (Kreidberg et al., 1993; Clugston et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kreidberg et al., 1993 and Clugston et al., 2006.

claim: The mechanism by which WT1 contributes to diaphragm development is still unknown.
source: However, the mechanism by which WT1 contributes to diaphragm development is still unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The G2 enhancer drives expression of Gata4 in the lateral plate mesoderm from the stage E7.5.
source: This enhancer drives expression of Gata4 in the lateral plate mesoderm from the stage E7.5, and by the stage E9.5 is active in the septum transversum and proepicardium, ceasing its activity by E12.5
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rojas et al., 2005 in the context of describing the G2 enhancer.

claim: By the stage E9.5, the G2 enhancer is active in the septum transversum and proepicardium, ceasing its activity by E12.5.
source: This enhancer drives expression of Gata4 in the lateral plate mesoderm from the stage E7.5, and by the stage E9.5 is active in the septum transversum and proepicardium, ceasing its activity by E12.5
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rojas et al., 2005 in the context of describing the G2 enhancer.

claim: The activity of the G2 enhancer is completely absent in the intermediate mesoderm.
source: The activity of this enhancer is completely absent in the intermediate mesoderm.
evidence: This is a statement about the G2 enhancer activity pattern that is presented as an established characteristic.

claim: In normal E10.5 embryos, the posterior and dorsal margin of the liver shows an accumulation of mesenchymal tissue, which extends from the dorsal mesenterium of the liver to the lateral tips of the lobes.
source: In normal E10.5 embryos, the posterior and dorsal margin of the liver shows an accumulation of mesenchymal tissue, which extends from the dorsal mesenterium of the liver to the lateral tips of the lobes (Figure 1).
evidence: This anatomical observation is supported by reference to Figure 1, which provides visual evidence.

claim: The mesenchymal layer at the posterior and dorsal margin of the liver is the PHMP described by Iritani (1984).
source: This mesenchymal layer is the PHMP described by Iritani (1984).
evidence: This claim connects the observed structure to a previously described anatomical feature, supported by citation.

claim: The PPFs, by E10.5 developmental stage, appear as a pair of outgrowths of the body wall located at both sides of the lung buds.
source: The PPFs, by this developmental stage, appear as a pair of outgrowths of the body wall located at both sides of the lung buds. (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This anatomical observation is supported by reference to Figure 1A,B.

claim: The PPFs are constituted of mesenchymal cells lined by the coelomic epithelium.
source: They are also constituted of mesenchymal cells lined by the coelomic epithelium.
evidence: This is an anatomical observation about the cellular composition of PPFs.

claim: The G2-Gata4 enhancer directed LacZ reporter expression in both PPF and PHMP at E10.5 and E11.5 in the mouse embryo.
source: The G2-Gata4 enhancer directed LacZ reporter expression in both PPF and PHMP at E10.5 and E11.5 in the mouse embryo (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No beta galactosidase activity was observed in the posterior and medial part of the septum transversum, where the liver is connected with the digestive tract.
source: However, no beta galactosidase activity was observed in the posterior and medial part of the septum transversum, where the liver is connected with the digestive tract (asterisk in Figure 1A), indicating that the G2 enhancer is not active in this specific domain.
evidence: This observation is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The G2 enhancer is not active in the posterior and medial part of the septum transversum where the liver is connected with the digestive tract.
source: However, no beta galactosidase activity was observed in the posterior and medial part of the septum transversum, where the liver is connected with the digestive tract (asterisk in Figure 1A), indicating that the G2 enhancer is not active in this specific domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of beta galactosidase activity observed in Figure 1A.

claim: PHMP and PPFs are not anatomically independent entities.
source: PHMP and PPFs are not anatomically independent entities.
evidence: This is an anatomical conclusion drawn from observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lateral tips of the PHMP appear continuous with the PPFs at the cephalic level while they are separated more caudally.
source: The lateral tips of the PHMP appear continuous with the PPFs at the cephalic level while they are separated more caudally (Figure 1B).
evidence: This anatomical observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The continuous part of the PHMP/PPFs ensemble apparently forms itself by the anterior growth of the peritoneal recess, which separates the liver sides from the body wall.
source: The continuous part of the PHMP/PPFs ensemble apparently forms itself by the anterior growth of the peritoneal recess, which separates the liver sides from the body wall.
evidence: This is an inference about the developmental process based on anatomical observations.

claim: The mesenchymal population of the ST originates the PHMP and also the most cephalic portion of the PPFs.
source: Thus, the mesenchymal population of the ST originates the PHMP and also the most cephalic portion of the PPFs.
evidence: This is an inference about developmental origins based on anatomical observations.

claim: The lateral closure of the pleural cavities occurs between E11.5 and E12.5 by posterior growth of the crescent-like continuum formed by the PHMP and the PPFs.
source: The lateral closure of the pleural cavities occurs between E11.5 and E12.5 by posterior growth of the crescent-like continuum formed by the PHMP and the PPFs, a process which is parallel to the fast growth of the liver lobes during these stages (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This developmental observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The lateral closure of the pleural cavities is a process which is parallel to the fast growth of the liver lobes during E11.5-E12.5 stages.
source: The lateral closure of the pleural cavities occurs between E11.5 and E12.5 by posterior growth of the crescent-like continuum formed by the PHMP and the PPFs, a process which is parallel to the fast growth of the liver lobes during these stages (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is an observation about the temporal relationship between two developmental processes, supported by Figure 1B,C.

claim: The PPFs continue posteriorly as the nephric ridges, the progenitor tissue of the mesonephros.
source: As seen in the Wt1Cre labeled cells, the PPFs continue posteriorly as the nephric ridges, the progenitor tissue of the mesonephros (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This anatomical observation is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: A loose mesenchymal tissue appears in the PPF between the more compact arrangement of the cells in the PHMP and in the renal ridges.
source: A loose mesenchymal tissue appears in the PPF between the more compact arrangement of the cells in the PHMP and in the renal ridges, but the commissural area of the PPF is always constituted by compact mesenchyme similar to that from the PHMP (arrow in Figure 2C).
evidence: This histological observation is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The commissural area of the PPF is always constituted by compact mesenchyme similar to that from the PHMP.
source: A loose mesenchymal tissue appears in the PPF between the more compact arrangement of the cells in the PHMP and in the renal ridges, but the commissural area of the PPF is always constituted by compact mesenchyme similar to that from the PHMP (arrow in Figure 2C).
evidence: This histological observation is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All mesenchymal populations in PHMP, PPFs, and nephric ridges are derived from a WT1-expressing cell lineage.
source: All these mesenchymal populations are derived from a WT1-expressing cell lineage, as shown by two models, the Wt1Cre;R26RLacZ (Figure 1B) and the Wt1Cre;R26RYFP (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: Expression of the Wt1 gene is revealed in the PPF and PHMP mesenchyme by the WT1-LacZ reporter and by immunohistochemistry.
source: Expression of the Wt1 gene is also revealed in the PPF and PHMP mesenchyme by the WT1-LacZ reporter and by immunohistochemistry (Figures 1C and 3A, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 3A.

claim: 80% of G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl embryos developed typical Bochdalek-type CDH.
source: 80% of G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl embryos developed typical Bochdalek-type CDH.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental study, supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Epithelial and mesenchymal cells of the PHMP and most anterior PPFs derive from a cell lineage in which Gata4 expression is driven by the G2 enhancer.
source: Epithelial and mesenchymal cells of the PHMP and most anterior PPFs derive from a cell lineage in which Gata4 expression is driven by the G2 enhancer. This is demonstrated by the expression of YFP in G2-Gata4Cre;R26RYFP embryos, and supports the existence of a process of cell migration from PHMP to PPFs (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The nephric ridges and the mesonephros derived from them show no YFP+ cells in the G2-Gata4Cre;R26RYFP model.
source: However, the nephric ridges and the mesonephros derived from them show no YFP+ cells in this model, indicating that the progenitors of these tissues derived from a different cell lineage.
evidence: This observation from lineage tracing experiments is used to infer different developmental origins.

claim: The progenitors of nephric ridges and mesonephros derived from a different cell lineage than PHMP and PPFs.
source: However, the nephric ridges and the mesonephros derived from them show no YFP+ cells in this model, indicating that the progenitors of these tissues derived from a different cell lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of YFP+ cells in nephric ridges and mesonephros in the G2-Gata4Cre;R26RYFP model.

claim: The gonad and the adrenal stroma were YFP+ in G2-Gata4Cre;R26RYFP embryos.
source: Interestingly, the gonad and the adrenal stroma were YFP+ (Figure 1G), and this can be related with the early expression of GATA4 in the coelomic epithelium, which will cover the genital but not the renal ridges (Figure 1H).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The GATA4 positive cells from the central part of the ST do not express YFP in G2-Gata4Cre;R26RYFP embryos.
source: Incidentally, the GATA4 positive cells from the central part of the ST do not express YFP in G2-Gata4Cre;R26RYFPembryos (Figure 1F), an observation consistent with the lack of reporter activity in the G2- Gata4LacZ embryos (Figure 1A).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1A.

claim: There is significant heterogeneity between central and lateral mesenchymal populations in the ST.
source: These data reveal a significant heterogeneity between central and lateral mesenchymal populations in the ST.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the differential expression patterns observed in the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: A clear asymmetry was observed in the distribution of PHMP mesenchyme in embryos of E10.5-E12.5.
source: A clear asymmetry was observed in the distribution of PHMP mesenchyme in embryos of E10.5-E12.5 (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Mesenchymal cells were always more abundant in the right PHMP than in the left.
source: Mesenchymal cells were always more abundant in the right PHMP than in the left, which might favor the herniation in the left side.
evidence: This observation is supported by quantitative image analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The R/L ratio of YFP+ cell volumes in PHMP was 1.21 and 1.45 in two E11.5 embryos, and 1.53 and 1.61 in two E12.5 embryos (mean = 1.45; S.E.M = 0.086).
source: We estimated, by image analysis, the volume taken up by the YFP+ cells in the right and left PHMP of four G2-Gata4Cre; R26RYFP embryos. The R/L ratio of these volumes was 1,21 and 1,45 in two E11.5 embryos, and 1,53 and 1,61 in two E12,5 embryos (mean = 1,45; S.E.M = 0,086).
evidence: This is quantitative data from image analysis experiments.

claim: The right PHMP contains about 50% more cells from the G2-Gata4 lineage than the left one.
source: Thus, the right PHMP contains about 50% more cells from the G2-Gata4 lineage than the left one.
evidence: This conclusion is based on statistical analysis of the R/L volume ratio data (t-test, p=0.0069).

claim: 36 out of 104 mutant embryos were included in the study.
source: We have included in the study 36 out 104 mutant embryos detected by genotyping.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design and sample size.

claim: Deletion of WT1 in the PHMP/PPFs continuum causes a phenotype characterized by defects in the inflow tract of the heart, coronary vessels and Bochdalek's hernia, most frequently located in the left side.
source: Deletion of WT1 in the PHMP/PPFs continuum, i.e. in the G2+ domain, causes a phenotype characterized by defects in the inflow tract of the heart, coronary vessels (Cano et al., 2016) and, importantly, Bochdalek's hernia, most frequently located in the left side (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and cited work (Cano et al., 2016).

claim: The genotypes of the embryos obtained at different ages show the expected percentage of mutants at all embryonic stages (about 25%) except for the stage E15.5.
source: The genotypes of the embryos obtained at different ages show the expected percentage of mutants at all embryonic stages (about 25%) except for the stage E15.5, when we only obtained four mutants among 60 embryos (Table 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by genotyping data presented in Table 1.

claim: At stage E15.5, only four mutants were obtained among 60 embryos.
source: The genotypes of the embryos obtained at different ages show the expected percentage of mutants at all embryonic stages (about 25%) except for the stage E15.5, when we only obtained four mutants among 60 embryos (Table 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from genotyping experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: Defect in the PHMP in G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos could be observed as early as E10.5.
source: We analyzed WT1 mutant embryos at different stages of development. Defect in the PHMP in G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos could be observed as early as E10.5, since less mesenchymal cells are present between the coelomic epithelium and the hepatoblasts when compared with control littermates (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This observation is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Less mesenchymal cells are present between the coelomic epithelium and the hepatoblasts in G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos at E10.5 when compared with control littermates.
source: Defect in the PHMP in G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos could be observed as early as E10.5, since less mesenchymal cells are present between the coelomic epithelium and the hepatoblasts when compared with control littermates (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This observation is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: At later stages, the closure of the pleural cavity by growth of the ST/PPFs crescent is delayed with respect to the controls in mutant embryos.
source: At later stages, the closure of the pleural cavity by growth of the ST/PPFs crescent is delayed with respect to the controls, and the mesenchymal cells of the PHMP are located more medially, not in the lateral tips of the liver lobes.
evidence: This is an observation from developmental analysis of mutant embryos.

claim: The mesenchymal cells of the PHMP are located more medially, not in the lateral tips of the liver lobes in mutant embryos.
source: At later stages, the closure of the pleural cavity by growth of the ST/PPFs crescent is delayed with respect to the controls, and the mesenchymal cells of the PHMP are located more medially, not in the lateral tips of the liver lobes. This is more evident at the left side (arrow in Figure 2E).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The medial location of PHMP mesenchymal cells in mutant embryos precludes caudal growth of the lateral commissures of the pleuroperitoneal septa and closure of the pleural cavities.
source: Thus, these cells cannot migrate towards the PPFs precluding caudal growth of the lateral commissures of the pleuroperitoneal septa and closure of the pleural cavities.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of CDH development based on the observed cellular distribution.

claim: Five E12.5 mutant embryos studied already showed strong reduction of the PHMP size as compared with control littermates.
source: Five E12.5 mutant embryos studied already showed strong reduction of the PHMP size as compared with control littermates, but the diaphragmatic defect of the WT1 conditional knockout embryos became clearly apparent by E13.5, when the pleural cavities are almost completely isolated in wildtype embryos (Figure 2F).
evidence: This observation is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The diaphragmatic defect of the WT1 conditional knockout embryos became clearly apparent by E13.5, when the pleural cavities are almost completely isolated in wildtype embryos.
source: Five E12.5 mutant embryos studied already showed strong reduction of the PHMP size as compared with control littermates, but the diaphragmatic defect of the WT1 conditional knockout embryos became clearly apparent by E13.5, when the pleural cavities are almost completely isolated in wildtype embryos (Figure 2F).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Of 23 mutant embryos analyzed by the stages E13.5 or older, only four of them showed normal development of the diaphragm.
source: Of 23 mutant embryos analyzed by the stages E13.5 or older, only four of them showed normal development of the diaphragm, while the rest of embryos showed different degrees of diaphragmatic defects (Table 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from phenotypic analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Three of the mutant embryos showed thin, membranous diaphragm in the left side.
source: Three of the embryos showed thin, membranous diaphragm in the left side and 16 showed a wide defect in the diaphragm, frequently with herniation of the liver into the left pleural cavity and hypoplasia of the left lung (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is quantitative data from phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 16 mutant embryos showed a wide defect in the diaphragm, frequently with herniation of the liver into the left pleural cavity and hypoplasia of the left lung.
source: Three of the embryos showed thin, membranous diaphragm in the left side and 16 showed a wide defect in the diaphragm, frequently with herniation of the liver into the left pleural cavity and hypoplasia of the left lung (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is quantitative data from phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: One mutant embryo (E13.5) showed the CDH defect only at the right side.
source: One of them (E13.5) showed the defect only at the right side and the CDH was present in the left side in the rest of them.
evidence: This is a specific observation from phenotypic analysis.

claim: About 80% of the E13.5 or older mutant embryos showed abnormal diaphragmatic development.
source: Thus, about 80% of the E13.5 or older mutant embryos showed abnormal diaphragmatic development.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the phenotypic data.

claim: Renal ridges appear well developed in mutant E11.5 embryos at a level corresponding to the entrance of the oesophagus into the ST.
source: Renal ridges appear well developed in mutant E11.5 embryos at a level corresponding to the entrance of the oesophagus into the ST (Figure 2E).
evidence: This observation is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The presence of intermediate mesoderm in thoracic renal ridges of mutant embryos was confirmed by ISH of Pax2.
source: The presence of intermediate mesoderm in these thoracic renal ridges was confirmed by ISH of Pax2 (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In wildtype embryos of the same age, thoracic renal ridges can be seen, but located more caudally, at the level of the stomach.
source: In wildtype embryos of the same age thoracic renal ridges can also be seen, but located more caudally, at the level of the stomach (Figure 1C).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The sharp boundary between the G2+ and G2− domains was clearly observed by the immunolocalization of WT1 and GATA4 protein in G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos.
source: The sharp boundary between the above explained G2+ and G2− domains was clearly observed by the immunolocalization of WT1 and GATA4 protein in G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos (Figure 3).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: WT1 immunoreactivity is strong in the PHMP and PPF of the wildtype embryos and localizes in the coelomic epithelium and, with a lower intensity, in mesenchymal cells.
source: WT1 immunoreactivity is strong in the PHMP and PPF of the wildtype embryos and localizes in the coelomic epithelium and, with a lower intensity, in mesenchymal cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT1 is clearly downregulated in the G2+ domain of the mutant embryos indicating an efficient excision of the WT1 floxed allele.
source: However, WT1 is clearly downregulated in the G2+ domain of the mutant embryos indicating an efficient excision of the WT1 floxed allele (Figure 3C).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C and is used to infer successful gene deletion.

claim: The presence of GATA4+ cells in the more cephalic part of the PPF supports a migration of PHMP cells towards the PPFs.
source: The presence of GATA4+ cells in the more cephalic part of the PPF supports a migration of PHMP cells towards the PPFs.
evidence: This is an inference about cell migration based on the distribution of GATA4+ cells.

claim: WT1 is involved in epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of the epicardium by repression of E-cadherin and activation of Snail1.
source: Since WT1 is involved in epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of the epicardium by repression of E-cadherin and activation of Snail1 (Martínez-Estrada et al., 2010), we checked the expression of E-cadherin in the developing PHMP of G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martínez-Estrada et al., 2010.

claim: Control E11.5 embryos show an E-cadherin negative coelomic epithelium over a layer of mesenchymal cells in the developing PHMP.
source: Control E11.5 embryos show an E-cadherin negative coelomic epithelium over a layer of mesenchymal cells in the developing PHMP (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Mutant embryos show expression of E-cadherin in the epithelium of the PHMP area and lack of E-cadherin negative mesenchymal cells.
source: However, mutant embryos show expression of E-cadherin in the epithelium of the corresponding area and lack of E-cadherin negative mesenchymal cells (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Systemic WT1 knockout mouse embryos do not survive beyond E13.5.
source: We have compared the G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl CDH phenotype with that displayed by the systemic WT1 knockout mouse embryos, which do not survive beyond E13.5.
evidence: This is a statement about the survival of systemic WT1 knockout embryos, representing established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Systemic WT1 knockout embryos show a more severe defect than G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl embryos, with a complete lack of PHMP.
source: Despite the early embryonic death of these models, we have observed a more severe defect, with a complete lack of PHMP and displaying, in some cases, persistent thoracic nephric ridges in E12.5 and E13.5 embryos (Figure 6).
evidence: This observation is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Some systemic WT1 knockout embryos display persistent thoracic nephric ridges in E12.5 and E13.5 embryos.
source: Despite the early embryonic death of these models, we have observed a more severe defect, with a complete lack of PHMP and displaying, in some cases, persistent thoracic nephric ridges in E12.5 and E13.5 embryos (Figure 6).
evidence: This observation is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In systemic WT1 knockout embryos, only the central part of the ST is conserved, i.e. the area where the G2 enhancer is not active.
source: In these embryos only the central part of the ST is conserved, i.e. the area where the G2 enhancer is not active, as shown in Figure 1E.
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 6.

claim: RALDH2 expression is found in the PHMP and PPF of wildtype E10.5-E11.5 embryos.
source: RALDH2 expression is found in the PHMP and PPF of wildtype E10.5-E11.5 embryos (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E,G.

claim: The PPF of the G2-Gata4Cre; Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos show an increased immunoreactivity for RALDH2.
source: The PPF of the G2-Gata4Cre; Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos show an increased immunoreactivity for RALDH2 but we found a reduced or absent expression of this enzyme in the PHMP (Figure 3F,H).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F,H.

claim: G2-Gata4Cre; Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos show reduced or absent expression of RALDH2 in the PHMP.
source: The PPF of the G2-Gata4Cre; Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos show an increased immunoreactivity for RALDH2 but we found a reduced or absent expression of this enzyme in the PHMP (Figure 3F,H).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F,H.

claim: RALDH2 is normally expressed at high levels in the intermediate mesoderm even in systemic WT1 knockout embryos.
source: In fact, RALDH2 is normally expressed at high levels in the intermediate mesoderm even in systemic WT1 knockout embryos, which also show decreased RALDH2 immunoreactivity in the liver mesothelium (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Systemic WT1 knockout embryos show decreased RALDH2 immunoreactivity in the liver mesothelium.
source: In fact, RALDH2 is normally expressed at high levels in the intermediate mesoderm even in systemic WT1 knockout embryos, which also show decreased RALDH2 immunoreactivity in the liver mesothelium (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: RA treatment partially rescues the pulmonary phenotype and promotes alveologenesis in the nitrofen model of induced CDH in rats.
source: RA treatment partially rescues the pulmonary phenotype and promotes alveologenesis in the nitrofen model of induced CDH in rats (Montedonico et al., 2008; Sugimoto et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montedonico et al., 2008 and Sugimoto et al., 2008.

claim: Five out of eight G2-Gata4Cre; Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos (62.5%) from RA-treated pregnant females displayed a complete septation of the pleural cavity by E15.5.
source: For ethical reasons we decided to limit the study to four litters in which we detected eight G2-Gata4Cre; Wt1fl/fl mutant embryos. Five of them (62,5%) displayed a complete septation of the pleural cavity by E15.5, i.e. about three times the proportion of normal phenotypes found in the non-treated mutants (Z test = 2,09, two-tailed p-value= 0,037).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the RA rescue experiment with statistical analysis.

claim: The proportion of normal phenotypes in RA-treated mutants (62.5%) is about three times the proportion found in non-treated mutants (Z test = 2.09, two-tailed p-value= 0.037).
source: Five of them (62,5%) displayed a complete septation of the pleural cavity by E15.5, i.e. about three times the proportion of normal phenotypes found in the non-treated mutants (Z test = 2,09, two-tailed p-value= 0,037).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of RA-treated and non-treated mutant phenotypes.

claim: Control littermates were not affected by the RA-treatment.
source: Control littermates were not affected by the RA-treatment.
evidence: This is an observation from the RA rescue experiment.

claim: Seven mutant embryos from three different females fed with control chow showed CDH.
source: Seven mutant embryos from three different females fed with control chow showed CDH (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the control group of the RA rescue experiment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Among nine mutant embryos from RA-supplemented diet, one showed normal diaphragm, three displayed CDH and five showed a small opening on the most posterior angle of the left pleural cavity.
source: For ethical reasons we decided to limit the study to four litters from females fed with RA-supplemented diet, where we identified nine mutant embryos. One of them showed normal diaphragm, three displayed CDH and five showed a small opening on the most posterior angle of the left pleural cavity (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the RA-treated group shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Two out of five control littermates from RA-treated females showed a small opening in the most posterior angle of the left pleural cavity.
source: Interestingly, two out of five control littermates also showed a similar opening in the same area (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the RA-treated control group shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The size of the diaphragmatic discontinuity was significantly smaller in the RA-treated mutants as compared with the control mutants (Student's t test, p-value=0.009).
source: The size of the diaphragmatic discontinuity was significantly smaller in the RA-treated mutants as compared with the control mutants (Student's t test, p-value=0,009), but it was no significantly different when compared with the defect of the two RA-treated controls (Student's t test, p-value=0,20) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of diaphragmatic defect sizes shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The size of the diaphragmatic discontinuity in RA-treated mutants was not significantly different when compared with the defect of the two RA-treated controls (Student's t test, p-value=0.20).
source: The size of the diaphragmatic discontinuity was significantly smaller in the RA-treated mutants as compared with the control mutants (Student's t test, p-value=0,009), but it was no significantly different when compared with the defect of the two RA-treated controls (Student's t test, p-value=0,20) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 7D.

claim: CDH could be caused by a defective population of the PHMP/PPF continuum by mesenchymal cells.
source: Our results suggest that CDH could be caused by a defective population of the PHMP/PPF continuum by mesenchymal cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis inferred from the experimental results.

claim: A process of migration of liver mesenchymal cells into the PPFs relevant for the closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal had been suggested in human embryos.
source: A process of migration of liver mesenchymal cells into the PPFs relevant for the closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal had been suggested in human embryos (Hayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hayashi et al., 2011.

claim: Left predominance of Bochdalek hernia can be connected with primary mechanisms of left-right visceral asymmetry, and particularly with an asymmetrical generation of mesenchyme.
source: Thus, we think that left predominance of Bochdalek hernia can be connected with primary mechanisms of left-right visceral asymmetry, and particularly with an asymmetrical generation of mesenchyme.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observed asymmetry in mesenchyme distribution.

claim: WT1 is required in the G2+ domain (PHMP and anterior part of the PPFs) for the formation of the pleuroperitoneal septa.
source: As we have shown, WT1 is required in the G2+ domain (PHMP and anterior part of the PPFs) for the formation of the pleuroperitoneal septa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing CDH in conditional WT1 knockout embryos.

claim: The immediate consequence of WT1 deletion in the G2+ domain is a lesser number of mesenchymal cells in the PHMP.
source: The immediate consequence of its deletion in this territory is a lesser number of mesenchymal cells in the PHMP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the histological observations in mutant embryos.

claim: WT1-null embryos completely lack PHMP.
source: Furthermore, WT1-null embryos completely lack of PHMP.
evidence: This observation is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6.

claim: WT1 is critically involved for EMT of the epicardium.
source: WT1 is critically involved for EMT of the epicardium (Martinez-Estrada et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martinez-Estrada et al., 2010.

claim: A hypothetical function of WT1 in the PHMP/PPF could be to promote EMT and generation of mesenchyme.
source: Thus, a hypothetical function of WT1 in the PHMP/PPF could be to promote EMT and generation of mesenchyme.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of WT1 in epicardium and the observed phenotype.

claim: The upregulation of E-cadherin concomitant with the lack of mesenchymal cells in the PHMP of the mutant embryos supports the suggestion that WT1 promotes EMT in this tissue.
source: The upregulation of E-cadherin concomitant with the lack of mesenchymal cells in the PHMP of the mutant embryos supports this suggestion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the E-cadherin expression data shown in Figure 5.

claim: WT1 plays the same role in the liver mesothelium as in the epicardium.
source: Furthermore, WT1 plays the same role in the liver mesothelium (Ijpenberg et al., 2007), and a recent report on the conditional deletion of β-catenin in the WT1 lineage leading to CHD (Paris et al., 2015) stresses again the relationship between WT1 and EMT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ijpenberg et al., 2007 and Paris et al., 2015.

claim: The loss of function of β-catenin phenocopies the loss of function of WT1 when its deletion is induced between E10.5 and E11.5.
source: Significantly, the loss of function of β-catenin phenocopies the loss of function of WT1 when its deletion is induced between E10.5 and E11.5, the time window in which we suggest that WT1 is promoting EMT in the coelomic epithelium of the PHMP.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the work of Paris et al., 2015 and is used to support the EMT hypothesis.

claim: The coelomic mesothelial origin of human diaphragmatic malformations, and their relationship with WT1 function were proposed by Suri et al. (2007) in a study on patients with Meacham syndrome.
source: The coelomic mesothelial origin of human diaphragmatic malformations, and their relationship with WT1 function were proposed by Suri et al. (2007) in a study on patients with Meacham syndrome, a rare multiple malformation affecting to genitalia, heart and diaphragm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Suri et al., 2007.

claim: Two out of eight patients with Meacham syndrome had heterozygous mutations in the zinc finger domains of WT1.
source: Two out of eight patients with this syndrome had heterozygous mutations in the zinc finger domains of WT1.
evidence: This is data from the study by Suri et al., 2007 on Meacham syndrome patients.

claim: G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mice, displaying congenital cardiac and diaphragmatic anomalies, can be a valuable animal model for Meacham syndrome.
source: Thus, our G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl mice, displaying congenital cardiac (Cano et al., 2016) and diaphragmatic anomalies, can be a valuable animal model for this kind of human pathology.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the mouse model based on phenotypic similarities to human disease.

claim: The presence of lateral plate mesoderm into the PPFs coincides with the backward movement of the intermediate mesoderm from the thoracic levels.
source: The presence of lateral plate mesoderm into the PPFs coincides with the backward movement of the intermediate mesoderm from the thoracic levels.
evidence: This is an inference about developmental processes based on the observed distribution of different mesodermal populations.

claim: Volpe et al. (2008) report increase of Hoxb4 expression in the nitrofen model of CDH.
source: Significantly, Volpe et al. (2008) report increase of Hoxb4 expression in the nitrofen model of CDH.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Volpe et al., 2008.

claim: Hoxb4 is a key gene to determine the nephric fate of the intermediate mesoderm.
source: This is relevant since Hoxb4 is a key gene to determine the nephric fate of the intermediate mesoderm.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of Hoxb4 that represents established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hoxb4 in anterior non-kidney mesoderm, either by retinoic acid (RA) administration or plasmid-mediated overexpression, resulted in ectopic kidney gene expression.
source: In fact, ectopic expression of Hoxb4 in anterior non-kidney mesoderm, either by retinoic acid (RA) administration or plasmid-mediated overexpression, resulted in ectopic kidney gene expression (Preger-Ben Noon et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Preger-Ben Noon et al., 2009.

claim: Nitrofen would preclude migration of PHMP mesenchyme towards the PPFs, leaving the intermediate mesoderm (which normally expresses HoxB4) in its primitive anterior position.
source: Our explanation for this paradox is that nitrofen would preclude migration of PHMP mesenchyme towards the PPFs, leaving the intermediate mesoderm (which normally expresses HoxB4) in its primitive anterior position.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed to explain the paradoxical Hoxb4 expression in the nitrofen model.

claim: WT1 has a dual function concerning the epithelial-mesenchymal transition and the reverse process, mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET).
source: WT1 has a dual function concerning the epithelial-mesenchymal transition and the reverse process, mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET).
evidence: This is a statement about WT1 function that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: EMT is promoted by WT1 in heart and liver (G2+ domain), but MET is induced by WT1 in the kidneys (G2- domain).
source: The first process is promoted by WT1 in heart and liver (G2+ domain), but MET is induced by WT1 in the kidneys (G2- domain) (Essafi et al., 2011) that lack a significant coelomic contribution (Ariza et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Essafi et al., 2011 and Ariza et al., 2016.

claim: Kidneys (G2- domain) lack a significant coelomic contribution.
source: The first process is promoted by WT1 in heart and liver (G2+ domain), but MET is induced by WT1 in the kidneys (G2- domain) (Essafi et al., 2011) that lack a significant coelomic contribution (Ariza et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ariza et al., 2016.

claim: GATA4 expression seems to be independent of WT1.
source: GATA4 expression seems to be independent of WT1 (Ijpenberg et al., 2007; Delgado et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ijpenberg et al., 2007 and Delgado et al., 2014.

claim: The involvement of GATA4 in CDH is probably related with the differentiation of the PHMP/PPFs mesenchyme and the migration of myoblasts during the late stages of diaphragm formation.
source: The involvement of GATA4 in CDH is probably related with the differentiation of the PHMP/PPFs mesenchyme and the migration of myoblasts (Merrell et al., 2015) during the late stages of diaphragm formation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about GATA4 function based on the work of Merrell et al., 2015.

claim: WT1 would be involved in an earlier developmental stage than GATA4, promoting the local generation of the PHMP/PPFs mesenchyme.
source: Instead, WT1 would be involved in an earlier developmental stage, promoting the local generation of the PHMP/PPFs mesenchyme.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the temporal role of WT1 in diaphragm development based on the experimental results.

claim: The Prrx1Cre;Gata4 fl/fl model shows bilateral CDH with membranous sac and defects of muscularization.
source: This explains differences between the Prrx1Cre;Gata4 fl/fl model of Merrell et al. (bilateral, with membranous sac and defects of muscularization) and our WT1 model, much more similar to the human Bochdalek hernia (left-sided and with discontinuity of the pleuroperitoneal septum).
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype from Merrell et al.'s work, used for comparison.

claim: The G2-Gata4Cre;Wt1fl/fl WT1 model is much more similar to the human Bochdalek hernia (left-sided and with discontinuity of the pleuroperitoneal septum) than the Prrx1Cre;Gata4 fl/fl model.
source: This explains differences between the Prrx1Cre;Gata4 fl/fl model of Merrell et al. (bilateral, with membranous sac and defects of muscularization) and our WT1 model, much more similar to the human Bochdalek hernia (left-sided and with discontinuity of the pleuroperitoneal septum).
evidence: This is a comparative assessment of the two mouse models based on their phenotypic characteristics.

claim: The claim made by Merrell et al. (2015) about the lack of contribution of the ST to the diaphragm should apply only to the central area of the ST where GATA4 expression is not driven by the G2 enhancer.
source: Incidentally, we think that the claim made by Merrell et al. (2015) about the lack of contribution of the ST to the diaphragm should apply only to the central area of the ST where GATA4 expression is not driven by the G2 enhancer, as shown by us.
evidence: This is a reinterpretation of Merrell et al.'s findings based on the authors' own data about G2 enhancer activity.

claim: Two types of CDH would originate in different moments of development.
source: In summary, two types of CDH would originate in different moments of development.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about CDH etiology based on the comparison of different mouse models.

claim: CDH due to defective generation of the PHMP mesenchyme appears in models of RA deficiency and also in models with loss of function of WT1.
source: CDH due to defective generation of the PHMP mesenchyme appears in models of RA deficiency and also in models with loss of function of WT1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different CDH models.

claim: In later stages CDH can develop by defective muscularization of the pleuroperitoneal septa.
source: In later stages CDH can develop by defective muscularization of the pleuroperitoneal septa.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about a second mechanism of CDH development.

claim: CDH by defective muscularization occurs in models of GATA4 conditional deletion and also in c-Met deficiency.
source: This type of CDH occurs in models of GATA4 conditional deletion (Merrell et al., 2015) and also in c-Met deficiency (Babiuk and Greer, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Merrell et al., 2015 and Babiuk and Greer, 2002.

claim: The dietary supplement of RA to pregnant females rescues pulmonary hypoplasia in the nitrofen model of CDH.
source: The dietary supplement of RA to pregnant females that rescues pulmonary hypoplasia in the nitrofen model of CDH (Montedonico et al., 2008; Sugimoto et al., 2008) was also partially effective in our model of conditional deletion of WT1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montedonico et al., 2008 and Sugimoto et al., 2008.

claim: RALDH2 immunoreactivity decreases or disappears in the PHMP of mutant embryos.
source: RALDH2 immunoreactivity decreases or disappears in the PHMP of mutant embryos, and this expression is probably activated by WT1 as it occurs in the epicardium (Guadix et al., 2006), where RA signaling is essential for epicardial EMT (von Gise et al., 2011).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: RALDH2 expression is probably activated by WT1 as it occurs in the epicardium.
source: RALDH2 immunoreactivity decreases or disappears in the PHMP of mutant embryos, and this expression is probably activated by WT1 as it occurs in the epicardium (Guadix et al., 2006), where RA signaling is essential for epicardial EMT (von Gise et al., 2011).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citation to Guadix et al., 2006.

claim: RA signaling is essential for epicardial EMT.
source: RALDH2 immunoreactivity decreases or disappears in the PHMP of mutant embryos, and this expression is probably activated by WT1 as it occurs in the epicardium (Guadix et al., 2006), where RA signaling is essential for epicardial EMT (von Gise et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to von Gise et al., 2011.

claim: The continuity between septum transversum, PPFs and nephric ridges suggests an evolutionary scenario about the origin of the diaphragm in mammals.
source: The continuity between septum transversum, PPFs and nephric ridges suggests an evolutionary scenario about the origin of the diaphragm in mammals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about evolutionary origins based on anatomical observations.

claim: The diaphragm probably derives from the cephalic end of the nephric ridges, which run throughout the peritoneal cavity in fish, amphibians and reptiles.
source: The diaphragm probably derives from the cephalic end of the nephric ridges, which run throughout the peritoneal cavity in fish, amphibians and reptiles.
evidence: This is an evolutionary hypothesis based on comparative anatomy.

claim: The thoracic nephric ridges were invaded in the ancestors of mammals by lateral plate mesodermal mesenchyme, giving rise to the pleuroperitoneal septa.
source: We suggest that the thoracic nephric ridges were invaded in the ancestors of mammals by lateral plate mesodermal mesenchyme, giving rise to the pleuroperitoneal septa.
evidence: This is an evolutionary hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The idea that PPFs derive from nephric ridges was already proposed by Goodrich (1930) based on purely anatomical observations.
source: In fact, the idea that PPFs derive from nephric ridges is not new. It was already proposed by Goodrich (1930) based on purely anatomical observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goodrich, 1930.

claim: The mesenchyme involved in the evolutionary replacement of nephric ridges by PPFs arises from the PHMP coelomic epithelium and this process is dependent on WT1 and RA.
source: We suggest that the mesenchyme involved in this process arises from the PHMP coelomic epithelium and this process is dependent on WT1 and RA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: WT1 has an evolutionary significance as a key factor involved in the origin of the diaphragm.
source: Thus, WT1 has an evolutionary significance as a key factor involved in the origin of the diaphragm.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the evolutionary role of WT1 based on the experimental findings and evolutionary hypothesis.

claim: The involvement of WT1 in the morphogenesis of the pleuropericardial septa had been described by Norden et al. (2010, 2012).
source: The involvement of WT1 in the morphogenesis of the pleuropericardial septa had been described by Norden et al. (2010, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Norden et al., 2010, 2012.

claim: Bochdalek's hernia could be regarded as an atavistic condition related with the failure in the ontogenetic/evolutionary process which replaced the thoracic intermediate mesoderm by lateral plate mesoderm expressing GATA4 under control of the G2 enhancer.
source: In summary, Bochdalek's hernia could be regarded as an atavistic condition related with the failure in the ontogenetic/evolutionary process which replaced the thoracic intermediate mesoderm by lateral plate mesoderm expressing GATA4 under control of the G2 enhancer.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about CDH as an evolutionary atavism based on the experimental findings and evolutionary scenario.

claim: WT1 was probably crucial in the process of generating the cellular substrate which made the evolutionary replacement of thoracic intermediate mesoderm by lateral plate mesoderm possible.
source: WT1 was probably crucial in the process of generating the cellular substrate which made this replacement possible.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary role of WT1.

claim: A right/left asymmetry in the process of mesodermal replacement is probably behind the left prevalence of CDH.
source: A right/left asymmetry in this process is probably behind the left prevalence of this disease.
evidence: This is a hypothesis connecting the observed asymmetry in mesenchyme distribution to the left-sided prevalence of CDH.

claim: The posthepatic mesenchymal plate coelomic epithelium gives rise to a mesenchyme that populates the pleuroperitoneal folds isolating the pleural cavities before the migration of the somitic myoblasts.
source: We show that the posthepatic mesenchymal plate coelomic epithelium gives rise to a mesenchyme that populates the pleuroperitoneal folds isolating the pleural cavities before the migration of the somitic myoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the developmental process based on the experimental observations.

claim: The process of mesenchyme populating the pleuroperitoneal folds fails when Wt1 is deleted from the PHMP area.
source: This process fails when Wt1 is deleted from this area.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phenotype observed in conditional WT1 knockout embryos.

claim: Mutant embryos show Raldh2 downregulation in the lateral mesoderm, but not in the intermediate mesoderm.
source: Mutant embryos show Raldh2 downregulation in the lateral mesoderm, but not in the intermediate mesoderm.
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mutant phenotype was partially rescued by retinoic acid treatment of the pregnant females.
source: The mutant phenotype was partially rescued by retinoic acid treatment of the pregnant females.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RA rescue experiments shown in Figure 7 and described in the results.

claim: Replacement of intermediate by lateral mesoderm recapitulates the evolutionary origin of the diaphragm in mammals.
source: Replacement of intermediate by lateral mesoderm recapitulates the evolutionary origin of the diaphragm in mammals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary significance of the developmental process observed.

claim: CDH might be viewed as an evolutionary atavism.
source: CDH might thus be viewed as an evolutionary atavism.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the evolutionary interpretation of CDH.
